1128.title: Rivers and seas
1128.hook: rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower (Tao Te Ching 66)
1128.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-six as a picture of servant leadership: the one who leads speaks humbly, stays behind, and does not compete for the front.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a hard chapter: two readings of the word simple. Your line was read it twice.

A good guide on a mountain trail walks in front, and nobody feels dragged. A good host fills the whole evening, and nobody feels crowded. A good coach is clearly in charge, and the players still feel it's their game. Chapter sixty-one, a few days back, used a low river to describe a great country. Chapter sixty-six brings the water back to describe one person who leads, and says the secret of those guides and hosts is the secret of the sea.
screen: `IN FRONT, BUT NOBODY DRAGGED.` → `THE WATER COMES BACK.` → `THE SECRET OF THE SEA.`

segments.voice: First, kings of the valleys. In James Legge's translation, rivers and seas receive the tribute of all the valley streams because of "their skill in being lower than they." They don't conquer the streams or call them. They're simply lower, so everything comes to them. The chapter calls that being king. Second, words below, steps behind. The sage who wants to be above the people puts his words below them; wanting to lead them, he puts himself behind them. An odd recipe for leadership: speak as if from underneath, walk at the back. Third, nobody feels the weight. When such a person is above, the people feel no burden; in front, they feel no harm. So the whole world is glad to push this person forward, and doesn't tire of it. Leadership, here, isn't grabbed. Others keep handing it to you, because you're easy to carry. Fourth, no contest. The chapter ends on a line the Tao Te Ching also uses in chapter twenty-two, which came up back on day nine hundred twenty-five: because this person doesn't compete, nobody in the world can compete with them. It looks like the manager who asks before she tells, the older sibling who lets the younger one go first, the expert who explains without making anyone feel slow. They lie lower, and everything finds its way to them.
screen: `KINGS OF THE VALLEYS.` · `WORDS BELOW, STEPS BEHIND.` · `NOBODY FEELS THE WEIGHT.` · then, large: `NO CONTEST, NO RIVAL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place where you're ahead of someone, older, more senior, or simply knowing more, and a moment there that's coming soon. Try the chapter's recipe on it: words below, a question instead of an announcement; steps behind, a place to let them go first. Find one small way to lie a little lower, and hold it gently.
Rivers and seas. In chapter sixty-six, they're king of the valley streams because they lie lower. Today's word.
Your line: they lie lower. That's why the streams come. Go gently.

pairs: no one can compete with you

1129.title: Three treasures
1129.hook: I have three treasures: compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first (Tao Te Ching 67)
1129.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep the three treasures of chapter sixty-seven, compassion, frugality and not pushing to be first, as a short daily checklist for how to carry themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rivers and seas: the sage leads by lying lower than everyone else. Your line was they lie lower.

Ask someone what they'd grab if the house were on fire, and you find out what they treasure. Photo albums. A grandmother's ring. The laptop. The dog, first, obviously. In chapter sixty-seven of the Tao Te Ching, the speaker answers a version of that question. The answer isn't a thing at all; it's three ways of carrying yourself through the world. And the third, at first hearing, sounds less like a treasure than a weakness.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU GRAB?` → `NOT THINGS: WAYS OF BEING.` → `THE THIRD SOUNDS WEAK.`

segments.voice: First, the list. In James Legge's translation: "The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others." Other translators say compassion, frugality, and not daring to be first in the world. Some readers hear in the first word a parent's tender love for a child. The second may sound familiar: frugal living came up just over a week ago. Second, each treasure opens a door. With gentleness, the chapter says, one can be brave. With economy, one can be generous. By not pushing to the front, one can become the leader of others. Courage grows out of tenderness, generosity out of thrift, and the one who hangs back is the one others end up following. Third, the warning. People now, the chapter says, give up gentleness and still try to be brave, give up economy and still try to be lavish, give up the back and push for the front. It says plainly where that leads: to death. A stark line. Fourth, the last word goes to the first treasure. Gentleness wins when it attacks and holds firm when it defends, and heaven guards a person with it. Day to day, the three are small and practical: a softer tone with a tired kid, not buying the thing to prove something, letting the other car merge. None of them would need carrying out of a burning house. Nobody can take them in the first place.
screen: `GENTLENESS, ECONOMY, NOT FIRST.` · `EACH ONE OPENS A DOOR.` · `DROP THEM, AND IT'S DEATH.` · then, large: `HEAVEN GUARDS WITH GENTLENESS.`

segments.voice: Hold each treasure for a few breaths, gentleness, then economy, then not pushing to be first, and ask where it could go today. Then choose the one that seems to have a place waiting for it. Rest with it, the way you'd keep a hand on something precious in your pocket.
Three treasures. In chapter sixty-seven: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. Today's word.
Your line: three treasures. The first one, gentleness, gets the very last word. Rest well.

1130.title: The good warrior
1130.hook: the best warrior isn't warlike; the best leader serves below (Tao Te Ching 68)
1130.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching, including students of martial arts and of leadership, take chapter sixty-eight as a portrait of calm strength: no rage, no showing off, and a leader who serves from below.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not pushing to be first. Your line was three treasures.

Chapter sixty-eight is short, and it reads like a job description written backwards. Wanted: a soldier who isn't warlike. A fighter who doesn't get angry. Someone good at winning who doesn't get drawn into the fight. A boss who puts himself underneath everyone he works with. It sounds like a list of people who'd be fired by Friday. The chapter says these are the skilled ones, and it gives the whole quality a name.
screen: `A SHORT CHAPTER.` → `A JOB DESCRIPTION, BACKWARDS.` → `THE WARRIOR WHO ISN'T WARLIKE.`

segments.voice: First, not warlike, not angry. The one skilled as an officer, the chapter says, is not martial, and the one skilled in fighting doesn't fly into a rage. Toughness that has to be shown off is easy to spot, and easy to push. And anger, whatever else it does, makes a fighter easy to read. Second, winning without engaging. The one good at overcoming opponents doesn't get tangled up with them. There's skill in not taking the bait, in letting the provocation pass by. Third, placing oneself below. The one good at using people puts himself below them: not giving orders from a height, but underneath, like the person holding the ladder while someone else climbs. That's the line behind today's carry. Fourth, the name. The chapter calls this the virtue of not contending, and the power of making use of others, and says it matches heaven, the highest standard of the ancients. Yesterday's three treasures included not daring to be first; some readers see today's warrior as that treasure carried into a fight. It's the shift lead who refills the supply closet, the parent who sits on the floor to talk at eye level, the team captain who carries the water bottles. Strong enough not to need to look strong.
screen: `NOT WARLIKE, NOT ANGRY.` · `WINNING WITHOUT ENGAGING.` · `PLACING ONESELF BELOW.` · then, large: `THE VIRTUE OF NOT CONTENDING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you lead, teach, look after, or simply have a little power over, and picture yourself holding the ladder while they climb. What do they need from below: time, a tool, someone to steady things? Let one answer come, and keep your breath steady, the way a good hand on a ladder stays steady.
The good warrior. In chapter sixty-eight, the one who isn't warlike, isn't angry, and puts himself below others. Today's word.
Your line: serve below. The ladder needs a steady hand at the bottom. That's today.

1131.title: A foot back
1131.hook: better to be the guest than the host, to retreat a foot than advance an inch (Tao Te Ching 69)
1131.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching, including students of strategy and the martial arts, take chapter sixty-nine as a teaching on restraint: answer rather than start, never underestimate the other side, and fight, if at all, with sorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the good warrior: not warlike, not angry, and placed below the people he leads. Your line was serve below.

Backing off has a bad name. Back down. Give ground. Retreat. Lose face. In a heated argument, the person who steps back first can look like the one who lost. Chapter sixty-nine of the Tao Te Ching quotes an old master of war, a man whose whole trade is fighting, and he chooses exactly that. He'd rather give up a foot than take an inch.
screen: `BACKING OFF HAS A BAD NAME.` → `A SOLDIER WHO PREFERS IT.` → `A FOOT BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the guest, not the host. The chapter quotes a strategist who doesn't dare to be the host; he'd rather be the guest. In Legge's reading, the host is the one who starts the war, and the guest is the one who answers. Then the line that names today, in Legge's translation: "I do not dare to advance an inch; I prefer to retreat a foot." Second, marching without marching. The chapter piles up strange pictures: advancing without seeming to move, baring an arm that isn't there, holding no weapon, facing no enemy. It's someone who refuses to give a fight anything to push against. Third, the worst mistake. No calamity is greater, the chapter says, than making light of the opponent; do that, and I come close to losing my treasures. Some readers hear the three treasures from two days ago: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. Legge reads it as gentleness. Underestimating the other side, in this picture, is how you lose your own gentleness. Fourth, the surprising winner. When armies meet, the side that grieves will win. Not the angriest, not the most confident: the one that is sorry there's a fight at all. Most days the war is smaller: a group chat, a dinner table, a parking spot. A foot back might mean letting the other person speak first, taking their point seriously, and caring that the two of you are at odds. That isn't losing. It's refusing to make light of anyone.
screen: `THE GUEST, NOT THE HOST.` · `MARCHING WITHOUT MARCHING.` · `NEVER MAKE LIGHT OF THE OTHER.` · then, large: `THE ONE WHO GRIEVES WINS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one disagreement that's live right now, and see the other person clearly, not as a cartoon. In your mind, take one foot back: let them speak first, and hear their point at full strength, not the weakest version of it. Then notice whether there's some sorrow underneath, that you're on opposite sides at all, and let it be there.
A foot back. In chapter sixty-nine, the old strategist would rather retreat a foot than advance an inch. Today's word.
Your line: a foot back. The side that grieves is the one that wins. Tomorrow: coarse cloth.

1132.title: Coarse cloth, jade inside
1132.hook: the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside (Tao Te Ching 70)
1132.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy's image of the sage, plain cloth outside and jade inside, as a picture of a life whose real worth is carried quietly rather than displayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a foot back: better to give up a foot than push forward an inch. Your line was a foot back.

A plain wool coat, a little frayed at the cuff. Nobody on the bus looks at it twice. Sewn into the lining, out of sight, is a small stone worth more than everything else the wearer owns. The coat isn't a disguise; it's just a coat. What matters is simply somewhere else. Chapter seventy of the Tao Te Ching ends on a picture very like that, and it gets there by way of a complaint.
screen: `A PLAIN COAT.` → `SOMETHING SEWN INSIDE.` → `THE CHAPTER'S COMPLAINT.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, the speaker says, and yet nobody in the world understands them or practices them. A strange thing for a book to admit about itself: the teaching is simple, and it still goes unused. Second, the reason. Words have an ancestor and deeds have a master, something they come from. People who don't know that root, the chapter says, don't know me either. Those who know me are few, and that makes what I carry precious. Third, the picture. So the sage wears coarse cloth, the rough garment of a laborer, and holds jade at the breast, the precious stone riding close to the body under cheap fabric. Notice what the chapter doesn't say. It doesn't say the sage hides the jade out of fear, or shows it off to the right people. The outside is plain, the inside precious, and the two don't have to match. Fourth, the jade in a life. Some of what's most valuable doesn't photograph well: a promise kept for years, a habit of noticing who's left out, a sentence someone said to you once that still steadies you. None of it needs a better coat. And a treasure that's always on display can start to be about the display. The question it leaves: what's your jade, and does it need anyone's eyes on it?
screen: `EASY WORDS, RARELY USED.` · `FEW KNOW THE ROOT.` · `PLAIN OUTSIDE, JADE INSIDE.` · `WHAT'S YOUR JADE?` · then, large: `COARSE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly: what's one good thing in my life I don't need to announce? A kindness you're doing, something you're learning, a thing you love that nobody else much cares about. Hold it without telling anyone, the way the sage holds jade under a rough coat, and if the urge to share it rises, let it settle.
Coarse cloth. Chapter seventy's picture of the sage: rough, plain clothing outside, precious jade carried close inside. Today's word.
Your line: jade inside. The coat can stay plain. That's today, done.

1133.title: Knowing you don't know
1133.hook: to know that you don't know is best (Tao Te Ching 71)
1133.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-one as a check on false confidence: being aware of the limits of what you know is counted the healthiest kind of knowing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was coarse cloth: the sage in a plain coat with jade held inside. Your line was jade inside.

A meeting. Someone asks a question across the table, and every head turns your way. You half know the answer. Maybe a third. There's a small, fast pressure to fill the silence with something that sounds right. Three short words would end it honestly, and in a room full of waiting faces, they can be hard to say. Chapter seventy-one of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built around those words.
screen: `A QUESTION ACROSS THE TABLE.` → `THE PRESSURE TO SOUND RIGHT.` → `THREE HARD WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. To know that you don't know is highest. Not to know, and to think you know, is a sickness. Two kinds of not knowing: one is aware of itself, the other is wearing a costume. Second, the turn. The chapter keeps playing with that word sickness. Only when you treat the sickness as a sickness, it says, are you free of it. The sage isn't sick, because the sage sees the sickness for what it is. Nobody is immune to pretending to know; the sage's health is just catching it. Third, a neighbor. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, and came away thinking he had one small edge on them: they thought they knew what they didn't, and he didn't think he knew. Two thinkers, far apart, arriving at the same door; neither is borrowing from the other. Fourth, where a real conversation starts. I don't know isn't the end of a conversation. It's where a real one begins. It lets the other person teach you, and it keeps a guess from hardening into a fact that others then build on. It's also a relief: you put down the work of seeming. Chapter seventy-one doesn't praise ignorance. It praises knowing where your knowing stops.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF NOT KNOWING.` · `CALL THE SICKNESS A SICKNESS.` · `SOCRATES LANDS THERE TOO.` · `WHERE A REAL CONVERSATION STARTS.` · then, large: `KNOWING YOU DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've been acting as if you understand: a topic, a person, a decision, maybe something about yourself. Silently, say to it: I don't know, and notice what happens in the body; some tightness may let go, some may grip harder. Stay with the open space those words leave.
Knowing you don't know. Chapter seventy-one: to know that you don't know is highest; to think you know when you don't is a sickness. Today's word.
Your line: I don't know. Three honest words. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1134.title: Don't crowd them
1134.hook: don't cramp people's homes or weary their lives (Tao Te Ching 72)
1134.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-two as advice on governing and on any kind of authority: don't press in on people's homes or lives, and they won't turn against you.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was knowing you don't know: being aware of where your knowing stops. Your line was I don't know.

A teenager's bedroom door, closed. On the other side, a parent with a question, a reminder and a worry, all lined up. Knock now, and the door may stay closed for a week. Wait an hour, and it might open on its own. Either side of that door is a hard place to stand. Chapter seventy-two of the Tao Te Ching is written to rulers, but it's about that hallway.
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR.` → `A QUESTION LINED UP.` → `KNOCK, OR WAIT?`

segments.voice: First, the warning. When people no longer fear what's fearsome, the chapter opens, something far more fearsome arrives. Pile on enough pressure and the pressure stops working, and what comes next is worse. Second, the instruction. Don't cramp the places where people live; don't weary the lives they lead. The old words are physical: don't press in on their dwellings, don't make them sick of living. Then a neat loop: only if you don't weary them will they not weary of you. Third, the sage's own room. The sage knows himself but doesn't put himself on show, and cares for himself but doesn't set himself up high. Someone who doesn't need to be seen, or to be above, has less reason to crowd anyone else. Fourth, the week, which ends here. Rivers and seas lead because they lie lower. Three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not daring to be first. The good warrior serves below. A foot back instead of an inch forward. Coarse cloth with jade inside. Knowing you don't know. Today fits the run: they're all ways of taking up less space so others have more. Room looks like a question asked once instead of three times, a plan left open for someone else to fill, not reading over a shoulder.
screen: `PRESSURE STOPS WORKING.` · `DON'T CRAMP THEIR HOMES.` · `NO NEED TO BE SEEN.` · `A WEEK OF TAKING LESS SPACE.` · then, large: `GIVE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Let your breath find its own pace, giving it room too, and bring to mind one person you've been pressing on, even gently: a child, a partner, a coworker, a friend who owes you a reply. Picture the space around them, and ask what you could stop asking, checking or reminding, just for today. Rest with the space that leaves.
Don't crowd them. Chapter seventy-two: don't cramp where people live or weary the lives they lead; if you don't weary them, they won't weary of you. Today's word.
Your line: give room. Less pressure leaves more space for them to come to you. Until next time.
